en: *Padacandrikā*. Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa! Having paid homage to the son of Umā, to Yājñavalkya, and likewise to my teachers.
The *Padacandrikā* is composed for the purpose of awakening [the understanding] of vowels (*svarādi*) and so forth. 1.
The high-pitched is to be known as *udātta*, while the low-pitched is *anudātta*; that which possesses both is *svarita*. *Pravāṃ* and *sva* are examples [of these]. 2.
A vowel, even if short, may be udātta, nīca, or svarita; likewise, long and protracted vowels are to be understood in the same way by those versed in the Vedas.
(3) I shall now declare the eight accents and their respective characteristics.
The *jātya*, the *abhinihita*, the *kṣaipra*, and likewise the *praśliṣṭa*;
the one known as *tairovyañjana* and likewise the *tairovirāmaka*;
the *pādavṛtta* and the *tāthābhāvya*: these are remembered as the eight *svaras*.
A *svāra* [svarita] that follows two consonants or two *yavamatras*, whether it is not preceded by anything or preceded by a low (*nīca*) tone, is called a *jātya* *svāra*. [Examples are:
*dhānyam*, *manuṣyām*, *cambī*, *vīryam*, and *kanyā iva*.
The *ukthya* sacrifice should be performed on the *pathyā* day, or it is said that one who was previously low [in status] becomes high in his own [state].

(7) Where there is the elision (*lopa*) of a high vowel *e*, *o*, or *ai* followed by a low vowel *a*, even if it is an *abhinihita* sandhi resulting from *pūrvarūpa*, it is a sublater of the *ādatta* sandhi. (8)
When a visarga, joined with a preceding vowel (upadhā), undergoes the change to *au*, and there is an *a* following it— as in the case where "vedo asi" is established—
the *u* following *e* or *o* certainly takes the form of the preceding sound (*pūrvarūpa*).
In those cases, the rule "vedo'si" serves as an illustration [of the exception].

At that time, the vowels *i* and *u*, when they are acute (*udātta*), become *y* and *v* respectively; however, when followed by an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel, they become *y* and *v* while remaining low-pitched (*nīca*).

The *svarita* accent shall be designated as *kṣaipra* in cases such as "vājyarvan," "tryambakam," and likewise "devye"; furthermore, there is the observation that it occurs in "sūnṛtā caiva" and "dvranno nvindraśca.
Moreover, the short vowel *i* may be acute (*udātta*), while the subsequent short vowel *a* is grave (*nīca*).
When those two [sounds] have become unified, it is called *svāra* and is designated as *praśliṣṭa*.
Whether in the case of "abhīndhatām," "divi," "vā," "api," "srucī," or "bhīmam," this should be understood in all such instances by the discerning experts of the Veda. (12–13)
A circumflex accent (*svarita*) preceded by an acute accent (*udātta*) and followed by a consonant is known as *tairovyañjana*; for example: *svānabhyāja yayā*.
Also, [the circumflex occurs] at the end of *ilā*, *iṃdra*, *dite*, *caṃdre*, *jyote*, *mahi*, and *viśruti*.

*Sarasvatī*, *tava agne*, and *ca havye kāmye gave hariḥ*—where there is an acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of a word-group (*avagraha*), and the following syllable is circumflex (*svarita*), one should know that as *taitro-virāma*; for example: *gomat prapra* and *gopatau*. 15–16.
Where a hiatus is observed between two *svarita* vowels, the *svarita* that follows it is called *pādavṛtta*. For example:
*dātra edhi*, *catā asya*, *navā'nukaḥ*, and *upa iti*. (17)
"What indeed were the gods?"—this is the illustration for "asanneva te" (as they truly were). 18.

That which begins with an acute accent (*udātta*) and ends with an acute accent, as well as that which is grave (*nīca*) and the *avagraha*, should be understood as having such a state; one should certainly pronounce a tremor (*kaṃpa*) there. 19.
*tanūnapāt*, *tanūnaptre*, and *tanūnapātam*—
these eight vowels are declared according to the Prātiśākhya [rules].
(20) Thus end the eight svarita vowels.
When a circumflex (svarita) vowel is combined with an unaccented (anudātta) vowel, it then becomes circumflex; therein the vision of Brahmā is created.
When it is combined with an acute (udātta) vowel, that [result] will certainly be acute.
One returns from the very quarters of the directions; here one meditates upon the Brahman as water.
2. A syllable following an acute (udātta) vowel becomes circumflex (svarita), provided it is unaccented (anudātta);
"For food thee" (iṣe tvā), "O Vāyu, that for us" (vāyavastannaḥ), and "Svāhā"—these are the illustrations. 3.
A circumflex (*svarita*) that precedes an acute (*udātta*) or a circumflex is suppressed;
this is seen in the case of *āghāye phalinīryāśca bhuvaḥ svariti*. Furthermore, after a circumflex, an unaccented (*anudātta*) syllable certainly becomes a protracted (*pracita*) tone.
5. "vājaḥ naḥ," "cāpraṇodyaḥ," and "chavyuptakeśāya" are instances where the *pracaya* accent is observed.
6. When a *pracaya* accent is placed before a *udātta* or a *svarita*, it does not occur; likewise, in "naḥ sūnuḥ" and "tathā yoṣāḥ kalyāṇyaḥ," such an observation is made.
The word *nīcaḥ* is not a *padānta*, and likewise, it is not *pracita* when followed by an *avagraha* where an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) accent follows. Similarly,
[the word] *devagaṇāḥ* and *prājāpatyaḥ* shine forth in that manner.
In the *tarat*, *abhīpāt*, and *senānya* [types of svarita], there is an illustration:
when a single syllable has become svarita in a word, having excluded that one [svarita] syllable, the remaining syllables are pronounced with the *anudātta* (low) pitch. 9.
Vāyu, Astūpara, Brahmā, Dhātṛ, Indra, Pūṣan, and Hari;
for the word *asmad*, the substitutes *naḥ*, *nau*, *me*, and *mā* are prescribed (10).
Indeed, the substitutes *tvā*, *vām*, *vaḥ*, and *te* are certainly established for the word *yusmad*.
The particles *ucit*, *samasmāt*, *marya*, *īmahe*,
*svit*, *sma*, *ha*, *vā*, and *cakam* (11), as well as *gha*— these are also unaccented (*anudātta*) when they function as particles (*nipāta*),
provided that the word *viveśa* is low-pitched (*nīca*) and has the sense of deliberation (*vicāra*). (12)

The final syllable shall have three morae (trimātra), while the following [syllable] does not possess three morae; for the purpose of investigation, there were two [syllables], and both of them indeed possessed three morae.
The preceding [syllable] should be udātta at the end, while the following [syllable] possesses total anudātta quality.
*Lāṃ*, *jī*, *ñchāṃ*, and *cī*—these, along with the *praṇava*, are all acute (*udātta*) accents.

The final syllable should consist of three morae (*trimātra*); this must be correctly understood by those learned in the Vedas. [The mantras] *bodha*, *ame*, *rocanā*, *ko’haṃ*, *pata*, *tvaṃ*, and *diva* likewise.
In the words *maṃhīya*, *īśa*, *īśānam*, *etāraḥ*, and *pāraḥ* (16),
as well as in these [following], this word always has its first syllable udātta:
*pātam*, *dhiyeṣitām*, *pratnām*, and *yajñasyodṛcaḥ* (17).
"Drink the honey-sweet [Soma], O Hotṛ, and likewise proclaim the Ṛta for the world and for the sacrificer; may the ageless ones [partake] of the oblation in the highest realms.
(18) In this [verse], the word *loka* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*), whereas elsewhere it possesses a completely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*) nature. (19)
Regarding the phrase "nābhir asya ṣaḍasya," the illustration is "guhāsyeti.
Because of the word "gṛbhīḥ" and the word "agni," there is a state of total anudātta (low pitch) for all [the syllables].
One should say "agnipūrvaṃ ghṛtena," which indicates a state of total anudātta for all [the syllables].

One who is both sinful and of evil speech is born entirely base. (21) When an address occurs at the beginning of a verse-quarter, or at the beginning of a non-verse-quarter, or when it does not have a distinct meaning [from the preceding], it receives the designation of *saṃbodhana* (vocative), which is invariably characterized by all syllables being unaccented (*sarvānudātta*). (22)
In the word *kadāriṣya*, the first syllable will certainly be udātta;
likewise, the word *kṛṣṇa* when denoting a deer is undoubtedly udātta on its first syllable.
Furthermore, in the sense of measure (*parimāṇa*), the word *mātrā* is udātta on its first syllable, as is *dakṣiṇā*.
Having sat down, [the word] *niṣadya* [is used]; likewise, *viśvakarmāsad* is used for the ten and the six.
Among these, *indra* protects; *dakṣiṇāt* has an acute accent (*udātta*);
*karṇaḥ* refers to one's own limb; *mahaḥ* is neuter; *skaṃdhaḥ* means valor; and the first letter is *a*. 24–25.
"Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ" [RV 1.89.8], "karṇau te" [RV 7.55.6], and "mahasthāndhasi" [RV 8.48.10]:
in these cases, the word *etā* denotes color and is invariably udātta on the first syllable; of this there is no doubt.
(26) In "rāyopoṣe tvā" [RV 10.121.10], it is seen that *irāya* is udātta on the first syllable.

The word *rāyaḥ* has its accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*), and it rules over its share through nourishment (*poṣeṇa*). (27) The word *tridhā* has its accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) when followed by *hita* and *baddha*;
furthermore, it has its accent on the first syllable when it expresses the sense of "well-done" (*sukṛtam*) and signifies "become" (*bhūta*). (28)
Even when the word *pāyu* follows, the suffix *an* is produced; however, after *ari*, *ama*, and *urvaśī*, it is necessarily udātta, and *āyu* would certainly follow.
(29) *Urvaśī-āyuḥ* and *aryamā-āyuḥ* exist; furthermore, after *āyu*, a *dvaṃdva* compound preceded by *soma* or *indra* is certainly and invariably udātta at its final syllable. (30)
This is an exception to the rule of double-accentuation (dvirudātta) when applied to *yam*, *iṣu*, *pūṣan*, *agni*, and *vāyu*;
however, when joined with the words *yaṃtrī* and *rāj*, as well as *rohita* alone, it is always invariably acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) provided it certainly denotes a color. 31.
Thus ends the section on vowels;
now begins the section on the accentuation of verbs (*ākhyāta-svara-prakaraṇa*).
When [a verb] occurs preceded by a word, provided it does not stand at the beginning of a metrical foot (*apādādau*).
One should state that which is not of different meanings as having all [its syllables] unaccented (anudātta).

The visualization [of the mantras] is as follows: "May we be invigorated by truth," "Drive away [the enemy]," and likewise, "Grant us a share in the lordship of cattle," and "O Viṣṇu, thou art the Veda. 2.

A verb preceded by a verb is invariably [accented] according to its original form (*prakṛti*); likewise, a verb following a vocative that is *ādyudātta* (acute on the first syllable) or *an-ita* (not having the augment *it*) is also [accented] according to its original form.
Examples are: *agne naya*, *tathā hotar yaja*.
This applies even from a vocative word consisting of a single syllable that is *ādyudātta*. (3–4)
By its very nature, that [verb] is called *prakṛti*; in some cases, it possesses total anudātta accent when there is no vocative word, and its meaning is also perceived as such.
In the Ṛgvedic verse "prajābhyas tvā," the verb remains in its *prakṛti* form.
That which follows the word *yat* and receives the designation "supreme" (parama) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
Furthermore, that [word] is understood even when it ends in any case-ending or even when it is a suffix;
whatever has a semantic connection with another, that belongs to it, even if it is situated at a distance.
For in truth, the immediate succession of those who lack the capacity is not the cause;
as the sages say of him whom they call Agni, so does Vāyu move him,
and others likewise eat what he has consumed, from which you, being unborn, shone forth.
Indeed, after the word *hi*, the subsequent verb should remain in its original form (*prakṛti*);

for instance, "for [he] was born" (*hy ajaniṣṭa*) or "thus [he] remains" (*tathāhisthet*). Others likewise desire this in the case of conjunction (*samuccaya*) of two verbs, where the first remains in its original form and the one following it likewise.
The second [type of person] is destroyed while standing in the midst of happiness; this is the illustration.
Furthermore, one who acts according to his own nature becomes like-minded with others. From the particle *na* and from the verb [root], it is called "nature" (*prakṛti*).
The particle *ca* (and) should be understood as indicating conjunction (*samuccaya*), or *vā* (or) as indicating deliberation (*vicāraṇā*).

Here, the word *tu* (but) indicates application (*viniyoga*), while *eva* (indeed) and *vā* (or) indicate restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Furthermore, when words such as *ha*, *eva*, or *ca* are not uttered, [the meaning is understood] from the context. 12–13.
If their meaning is somehow understood there, it is [explained] by the verbal root; however, this is established in the Vedic commentary as follows:
"He honors the Maruts, and the songs bestow light and vision."
Śivā, Apayavatī, Suṣadā, and Madhumatī; 15.
Also Yattena, Adhṛṣṭa, Ojasvān, Bhrājasvān, Śuṣmiṇī, Bhrājasvān, Bhadravācyāya, Vedyo, Medhyo, Yama, and Trita. 16.
In these words— *svasā*, *ādityaḥ*, *somena*, and so forth, as well as in the subsequent ones ending with *dhana*, *dāra*, and *ratna*— the word *asi* (sword) would have its first syllable udātta;
and in nineteen instances, *asi* has its first syllable udātta without doubt.
Among the twenty prefixes, nine have the acute accent on the final syllable (e.g., *pra*, *parā*, etc.),
ten have the acute accent on the initial syllable (e.g., *anu*, *upa*, etc.), and one, namely *abhi*, has the acute accent on the final syllable.
A prefix that would otherwise be unaccented becomes accented when followed by another prefix in a compound (*upasarge pare vṛtti*).
The same applies when *saṃ* is followed by *prayātam*, as well as *saṃpracyavadhvam*;
and when it occurs before a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, or when it stands before an acute-accented (*udātta*) vowel—such as in *saṃbharam*, *syapiva*, and *ati*. (20)

When a word is repeated (*āmreḍita*), the latter [form] should be used; every [particle] such as *ni*, *caratu*, *niścitaṃ*, *upa*, *upa-īta*, *saṃsam*, *ica*, *eva*, *pra-prāya*, and *iti*—this is the rule for the observation [of these].
Thus ends the section on verbs and prefixes (*ākhyātopasarga-prakaraṇa*).
When *ca* and *cha* follow, the substitution of *ś* occurs for the *visarga*,
as in "vājaśca" and "prasavaśca"; likewise, when *ta* and *tha* follow, the substitution of *s* occurs for the *visarga*, and the *paṅkti* meter is also not perceived.
The *aṃ* and *aḥ* [substitutes] and the gods (*devāḥ*) are the illustrations.

When followed by *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*, as well as by *k*, *kh*, *p*, and *ph*, the *visarga* remains in its original form (*prakṛti*); however, in the alternative case (*pakṣe*), it certainly becomes *ardha-* [visarga] before letters beginning with *ka*. (2–3)
*Mitraḥ śaṃ varuṇaḥ śam*, *apy aditiḥ ṣoḷhā*,
and *devo vaḥ savitā*— these should be on the right wing in sequence;
likewise, *naḥ kalpam* and *tām*, and then *svanemaniścitaṃ*.

The *visarjanīya* of the word *saḥ*, when followed by a consonant, is elided; furthermore, the *sakāra* of *sapituḥ* and *sanaḥ* likewise becomes *sakāra*. (5–6) *Phalinīḥ* and *cayāḥ* [are examples], as well as *pakṣe* and *ardha-visarjanam*.
(5) [The rule] "of that (*saḥ*)" applies even when the *visarjanīya* stands before a consonant; moreover, the *sakāra* of *sapituḥ* and *sanaḥ* also arises [as *sakāra*]. (6)
The visarga is certainly elided after the letter *s* when followed by *t* and *th*; this is seen in the examples *tad viṣṇu stavate* and *am̐dhastho vāyava stha*.
Similarly, even a double visarga is elided after the word *pīvaṃ* when *upa-vasane* follows.
In the case of *saḥ*, the visarga is also elided before the two words *tvoṣadhī*.
However, the elision of *sya* occurs before *eṣa* and *iṣa* when a consonant follows;
examples of this are *syarāthyasya*, *vājī*, and *tveṣate*.

The *visarga* preceded by a guttural (*kaṇṭhya*) becomes *s*, and the subsequent *visarga* becomes *ṣ*. From this point forward, by virtue of the governing rule (*adhikāra*), there are also [the following]:
*ilāyāḥ*, *varivaḥ*, *celaḥ*, *api-āviḥ*, and likewise *nirvasatiḥ*.
In these six instances, the *s* becomes *ṣ* in sequence:
(1) in *div-okaḥ*, (2) in *pṛthivyāḥ*, (3) in *rāyaḥ*, (4) in *sahasraḥ*, (5) in the *visarga* of these two [i.e., *rāyoḥ* and *sahasroḥ*], and (6) in *poṣa-putrayoḥ*. 11–12.
To Sūrya, the son of heaven; on the back of heaven, the expansive one;
"from the back of heaven, from heaven, from Parjanya"—this is the illustration (13).
From heaven and from earth, Agni is the vigor; he is the head of heaven, the summit of heaven.
With the increase of wealth, O Son of Strength, may we be united.
Beyond the emission of darkness, in the highest station, beyond the darkness of the beginningless and even beyond the dispelling of darkness— 14–15.
In *riṣas-pṛśaḥ* and *rajasaḥ-dhanaḥ*, [the final vowel] remains as it is when followed by the root *pā*;
here, the inclusion of the verbal root *pā* is illustrated by the example *riṣas-pātu*.
In *tapasaḥ-pṛthivī* and *śabde-satvam*, [the final vowel] likewise remains as it is when followed by *adhi* and *anaska*. (16)
From heaven it shines forth through the heat upon the earth; make a path!
(17) When they occur in the same word, *sa* and *ṣa* may be used for the *visarga*; likewise [the forms] *bhūyaskaraḥ*, *cakṣuṣpāḥ*, and *pathaspathaḥ* are for the purpose of clarity. (18)
But after a harsh [consonant], the *visarga* becomes *satva*, provided there is no subsequent harsh consonant;
and in the word *paruṣa*, as in *paruṣaḥ paruṣaḥ pari*,
when the word *pari* follows, and likewise in *vasāna-sthe*, *kaviḥ*, *kara*, and *kṛdhi*.
And in the case of others, there is the substitution of *s* for *visarga*, while the substitution of *ṣ* occurs in due order:

"oṃ ṣadhayaspari" (instead of *oṃ sādhyāḥ pari*), "paruṣasparuṣaspari" (instead of *paruṣaḥ paruṣaḥ pari*), "noṃvasyasaskaraccaiva" (instead of *no vasyaḥ askaraccaiva*), "punaskṛdhi" (instead of *punaḥ kṛdhi*), and "vasuṣkaviḥ" (instead of *vasuḥ kaviḥ*). 20–21.

The *satva* of *kṛṣi* occurs only before *kṛdhī*; *kṛṣī* and *kṛdhi* are well-established, as are *sadyo* and *dyauḥ*, and these [forms] occur when the path of the father (*pitṛpatha*) has been made. (22) Furthermore, the *visarga* becomes *sakāra* and *ṣakāra* in *sadaskṛtam*.
Likewise, in "dyauṣpitā" and "namaspathaḥ," the *dhruva* [anusvāra] occurs; 23.
when the word *pati* ends in the sixth case (genitive), the *visarga* becomes a *satva* (anusvāra);
as in *vācaspatim*, *viśvakarmāṇam*, *pūṣaṇam*, and *brahmaṇaspatim*. 24.
The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs when followed by future [sounds] and when situated within the same word (*samānapada*), as in *sīṣayāma*, *asuṣāva*, *goṣṭhānam*, and *parameṣṭhī*. Furthermore,
the substitution of *ṣ* occurs even when there is an intervention by a *visarga* following future sounds.
Indeed, when there is a *samāna* vowel and a consonant, it results in a good dream (auspiciousness).

(26) The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* is prescribed after an *anusvāra*, a nasal (*aṅga*), or the letter *v*, as in *tapūṃṣy agne havīṃṣy ā*; this should be understood by Vedic scholars in other instances as well. (27)
There shall be the substitution of *ṣ* for the *k* of *kāra*, as well as for the root *sīdati* when preceded by *ni*;
likewise for *sasāda* when preceded by *ni*, as in *niṣasāda* and *niṣīdataḥ*. There is also the substitution of *ṣ* for *su* after the word *mo*, as in *moṣūṇa*.

From the indeclinable *ukāra* (the syllable *u*), there is the substitution of *su*, and there is also the substitution of *ṣ*; likewise, there is *uṣūṇa*. There shall be the substitution of *ṣ* for the word *su* when it follows *abhi*; however, [the form] is *abhīṣuṇaḥ*.
Furthermore, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for the root *siñcati* (to sprinkle) when preceded by *pari*, as in *pariṣiñcati*, and also when preceded by *abhi*.
The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs only after [the prefix] *siṃcate*; thus we have *abhiṣiñca* and *abhijāyate*.
However, when there is an intervention by the vowel *a*, as in *abhyaṣiñcan* and *yābhir eva*, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur.
According to you, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* would occur after a prefix, as in *viṣyāmi* and *viṣyatu*.
From this point forward, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, and likewise *ṭ* and *ṭh* for *th* when followed by *math* and *yaḥ*.
Indeed, because of the word "hi," there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* when *math* and *yaḥ* follow; however, there is the substitution of *ṭh* for *th* [in the following]:
*hiṣmāte*, *tvāpo hiṣṭhāḥ*, and *mayo bhuvaḥ*. 32–33.
After the word *dyavi*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* [of the suffix]; when followed by *th*, *ṭh* is substituted [for *t*].
After *nis*, there should be the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, and likewise *ṭ* for the following *t*.
Thus: *tatakṣau*, *niṣṭatakṣuḥ*; and likewise after *nis* in the case of *casti* and *āyateḥ*.
*Sadhiraṃśuḥ*, *āditiḥ*, *mākiḥ*, *vandāruḥ*, and *eva*—in these, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* and *ṭ* for *t* in the following word:
*sadhiṣṭavat*, *āśuṣṭe*, *tvādiniṣṭvā*, and likewise [others]. (35–36)
May no affliction overcome you; may the pair of the wrathful ones be well-established for you.
In the single-syllable [mantra], *ṣatva* belongs to Vāyu, and *caṭa* belongs to Agni and Viṣarga.
Vāyu is indeed your overlord, and likewise Agni is your overlord.
In the presence of a single consonant, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarga*, and the following *ṭa* [is substituted for *ta*]. (38) [Examples include:
*bṛhaspatiṣṭvā sumne*, *ca patiṣṭvāsādayatu*, as well as *pāyubhir mātṛbhiś caiva*, and *varūtrīr arcibhis tathā*. (39)
In these cases, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the suffix *visarga*; for that [substituted *ṣ*], *ṭ* and *t* may optionally occur:
*vāyubhiṣṭvam*, *mātṛbhiṣṭvam*, *varūtrīṣṭvā*, *arcibhiṣṭvasu*.
Furthermore, in the case of the root *sah* following *pṛtanāyāḥ*, the *s* becomes *ṣ*, as in *pṛtanāṣāṭ*.
Thus ends the section on *visarga*.

Now begins the section on the prohibition of *satva* and *ṣatva*: "May he whose thighs are firm follow the sacrificial ground of Bṛhaspati’s son, which is very large and rich in excellent crops; may he who has beautiful joints [follow] the one who is fair to behold."
May they enter well-kindled [fires] with intentness; may the cow-winning [sacrifice] be successful.
With the pestle, the two tawny ones, and with lead, [may one reach] that which touches the sky.
Lead, touching the sky, [is] the wife; may the offerings be joined together, winning cattle.
*Pratisadṛṅ*, *hīsīścaḥ*, and likewise *pratisadṛkṣāsaḥ*;
*pṛthivicarṣaṇīyāsi*, *śakuni*, and *upari vai divi*—in these cases, it is certain that the change to *ṣatva* does not occur for the following *s*. 4.
From the *prakṛtis* and from the *parisads*, and likewise from the *pṛthivī-sad*— may you go and establish yourself among the *divi-sad*s and the *carṣaṇī-sahas*.
With that [power] of the bird-seated one, the other reading is indeed impure.
There are three [syllables] for the tittiri-bird, and those same three for both the Ṛc and the Sāman.
With the *antaḥpārśvya* [breath], there is the Vājapati, as well as the *edidhiṣu*;
by means of the *antaḥparśavya*, there is no *ṣa* in the release (*visarga*) of these.
The word *vāsaḥ* (garment) becomes *palpūli* when followed by *ekaṃ*; likewise, the word *parivājapatiḥ* (the lord of wandering mendicants) and *kaviḥ* (the sage).
Furthermore, there is a prohibition regarding one who has already reached [the state], as is the case with the *aididhiṣu-patiḥ* (the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried).
In the word *patau*, the vowel *aḥ* and the visarga also undergo the change to the letter *r*.
Only very brief examples have been stated here for fear of excessive prolixity;
where doubt arises, one should consult the *Prātiśākhya*.
Thus ends the section on the prohibition of *satva* and *ṣatva*.

The section on elision and augmentation is now being stated; from this point forward, elision and augmentation, as well as the modification of a letter and the substitution of a retroflex for a following [dental], will be discussed.
When the word *svardhūḥ* occurs, its visarga becomes a *repha* (the sound *r*).
In the case of *sāṃsahoḥ*, there is a cerebral [substitution] for both [sounds], and for the subsequent [sound] as well;

however, in the case of *svarṣām* and *appāṃ* belonging to the Kāṇva school, the form *dhūrvāhau* arises, whereas in the Mādhyandina school it is *dhūrṣāhau*; this [rule] is intended with reference to that [latter case].

Even for the visarga of *duḥ*, when the vowel *ū* follows, there is the substitution of the retroflex [sibilant] for the subsequent [visarga]; likewise for *dū* and *labh* followed by *ra*. Furthermore, when *duḥ* is followed by the letter *da*, it becomes *utva* (the substitution of *u*).
But for another [word], the cerebralization occurs in the case of *mūrdhan*, as well as in the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and the oblations (*havīṃṣi*).
Furthermore, when the word *vāh* follows, the change of *s* to *ṣ* occurs in *anaḥ*;
likewise, we shall follow the ox, both in the form *anaḍvān* and *anaḍvāham*.
From the word *āghā*, the letter *t* becomes *ṭ*, as in *dārvāghāṭa*;
likewise, the word *vana* with the letter *s* becomes *vanaspati*. The word *vana* is separated from the word *sad* by the letter *r*.
And when the word *sade* follows *veṭa*, there would be no *lakṣya* for *vanarṣadaḥ*. When *patau* follows, there is an intervention by the vowel *ṛ* and the letter *au*;
this applies specifically according to the numerical order, as in *ṛtaspate* and *varasya*.

In the word *bṛhatas*, there shall be elision of the letter *t*; however, in the case of *taskara* and *bṛhaspati*, there is an intervention by the letter *s* when [the suffix] *kare* or *patau* follows.
The word *pari* is not separated [from the following consonant] when the sound *kṛta* occurs, even when the substitution of *ṣ* takes place.

The word *su* [as a prefix] before *candra* and *sarpiṣ* is not separated by anything; however, when both *su* and *candra* follow *sarpiṣ*, they are refined [by sandhi]. Furthermore, the letter *dh* belonging to the word *dudhukṣan* undergoes the change to *d*. 11–12.

Thus ends the section on elision and augmentation. Now begins the section on the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva): after retroflex consonants (*ṛṣar*) and when the preceding word is the same, the dental *n* becomes *ṇ*.

The examples are "pitṝṇām," "nṛṇām," "pūṣṇaḥ," and "pūrṇam. An intervention may also occur by means of the *ka*-group, the *pa*-group, vowels, or the letters *ya*, *va*, and *ha*, whether these are used individually or collectively.
And Nṛmaṇas with the strainer, likewise Purīṣavāhana for the ritual act, and Pravāhaṇa for Varuṇa and the two [others], and the vision;
Indra leads him forth for the one who is seated, protecting him.
In *suṇāsatyāsuṇatva*, *svarṇāsthūriṇaśca*, and *samindraṇaḥ* (4), there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*.
In *praṇa āyūṃṣyuruṣyāṇaḥ* and *pariṇorathavāhaṇam* (5),
there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* after the prefixes *pra-* and *pari-*, and optionally the substitution of *ṇ* for *m* in *prahiṇomi*.
After a prefix (upasarga) that begins with a non-udātta vowel, the *ṇ* replaces the *n* of the root *ni*;
thus one says *praṇaya*, *praṇayantu*, *praṇudan*, and *praṇudati*.
This substitution occurs even in the absence of [the specific conditions mentioned in] these very rules.

Due to the restrictive rule that [the substitution] occurs nowhere else, the mention of *pūṣan* is not subject to the change; thus, according to the opinion of Kātyāyana, the substitution of *ṇ* in *pariṇaḥ* and *śrīmaṇāḥ* occurs, and furthermore,
a *n* at the end of a word remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*) as in *pitṝn*.

The *vādhraśnasa* and the two *babhru* [verses] are naturally [in the *gāyatrī* meter]; likewise, the *dhruva* [verse], "O Indra and Agni, of wondrous luster," the *vārtraghna*, and the *duḥṣvapnya* [verse] are also [of that nature].
Furthermore, there is the *dhruvayoni*, the *brahmavani*, and the *āyaspoṣavani*.
The *puronuvākyās* [are recited] with the sound of a skin-drum, or as a throat-clearing sound.
Thus ends the section on the substitution of *ṇ*. Now begins the section on long vowels.
In *arcā*, *atiṣva*, and so forth, the first syllable is udātta; furthermore, in *saṃhitā*, the vowels *ī* and *ū* are certainly long in *nīhāreṇa*, *nīvāra-ruvan*, and *anavagraha*.
Also, in *yojānu-dhārayāmā* and *yajāno-vā na ātunaḥ*, [the same applies].
*gāyata*, *naraḥ*, *uṣuṇaḥ*, *apyuruṣyāṇaḥ*, and likewise *rakṣaṇāḥ*, *sacasvānaḥ*, *yacchānaḥ*, *jayatānaraḥ*,
*matsadhānaḥ*, *pipṛtāni*— after the letter *n*, when followed by the vowel *au* or the consonant *p*, [the preceding *n* becomes *ṇ*]. 3.
When *yajānaḥ* and *bhavānaḥ* are followed by a word beginning with the letter *n*, as in the case of *yoja* and other such words, their vowel lengthening is certain;
this also applies to the words *avarūtha-vājyasya* and *pāyuṣveṣu*.
The word *bhava* is long [only] when followed by *syām*; it is certainly not so in any other case.
When the word *su* follows, the word *ukāra-upṛkta* (containing the vowel *u*) becomes long, as in *ūṣuṇo* and *ūṣuṇāsatyā*, but not otherwise, nor in *uditiṣva*.
In the words *udāritha*, *salakṣmādya*, *śocapanayasādaya*, and *bhavatādyāśca*, as well as in the case of the letter *ya*, lengthening occurs; hear these examples: *tāvatiṣu*, *arakṣat*, and *api*.
When followed by the letter *m*, the six words [ending in *-as*] become long. When followed by *hā* or *ca*, the word *tvaghaśabda* becomes long.
[The same applies when followed by] *vṛṇīmahe*, *ca*, *devāśva*, *bhavatā*, and other [words]. 9.
In *vāje ādyāḍhuva*, *api avo adya vṛṇīmahe*,
*adyā ca mṛlayāpi evam tvadyā devān ahotari*,
and *te pūṣṇo jahimaśca*— in these word-forms, there is lengthening (*dīrghatām*).
In this context, they say that in the words *cātra*, *atrātre*, *apūṣṇo*, *trā jahī*, *naraḥ saptaṛṣīn*, *nāstaḥ*, and *niyudbhiḥ*,
there occurs the lengthening of the vowel of the word within these specific positions.
Thus, when these [vowels] are followed by a consonant, they indeed undergo lengthening; furthermore, the beginning of a quarter-verse (pāda) is also taken as such.
We know that the lengthening of the word *vidma* occurs in the *Asautrāmaṇī*, but [only] before a consonant.
The lengthening of the word *adha* occurs in *adhā hy agne*, *adhā yathā*, and *adha*;
the lengthening of the nasal (*n*) occurs before *yat*, *gnāḥ*, *asmat*, and *vāyuṣu*.
(14) [In the verse] *pibā sutasya hiṣmā te varddhayā rayim eva ca*.
Hear our invocation and grant us wealth; hear also, O pressing-stones.
Drink the Soma and yoke your horses, for you are the one who brings strength in the battle. May you protect us from heaven as we ascend the wood for our well-being; drink also.
Open wide for us in the invocations; hear our songs!
Bending your knees, lick the earth, and overcome our enemies. Accept the oblations; be mindful of us and produce waters for us.
May we succeed in our training with our friends; thus may we present it to you.
Let us proclaim even the crossing of the clarified butter; may you cause us to go beyond darkness.
By means of which [hymn] you have traversed the highest [realm], pour out the pressed juice with the *asamṛt* verse. 19.
Protect our offspring; worship the gods with oblations and with a chariot;
and with that purifying vision by which Saramā found the way, may you provide guidance for us in our sacrifice and grant us freedom from old age.
Pretā, Ajayatāt, Aratā, Sakhāyaḥ, Bhūṣaṇas, Tathā;
Suṣṭarīmā, Juṣāṇaḥ, Varddhaya, Tvam, Tathaiva Ca; Kṣāmābhiṃdata, Eva Api, Sṛjārarāṇa, Eva Ca. 21–22.
O wise one with beautiful tongue, bring us strength; make our speech sweet and cause it to flow evenly.
May we both be protected and may wealth be sustained for us. O guardian, protect us and grant us riches.
In the *saṃhitā*, however, there shall be lengthening for these [words] when followed by a word [beginning with a vowel]: *vīraḥ*, *viśve*, *vājayaṃtaḥ*, *vṛtram*, and likewise *vikhyeṣam*.
But there is no lengthening of the final syllable of *abhipadaḥ* when these [words] or others follow.
The word *ava* is not lengthened when followed by *na* or *yāmi*;
the word *adya* is not lengthened when followed by *na* or *yāmi*; and the word *adya* is not lengthened when followed by *hotarye* with *va* following it. 25.
Thus ends the section on lengthening.
Now begins the section on the addition of the *anusvāra*:
the substitution of *ś* for *n* occurs even when followed by *c* or *ch*.

Therefore, even a preceding *anusvāra*, as well as an augment (*āgama*), is prescribed. "Pruṣīdga" for "cakṣuṣe," and "tvahadga" serves as an illustration; there would be no state of having an *ṛ* vowel when *t* and *th* follow. (1-2)

The *anusvāra* arises precisely before the letter *s*; furthermore, the examples are "anyāt," "garat," "paśūn," "udgātā," and "tāvat. When the letter *p* follows, the *visarga* of the letter *n* in the word "nṛ" [is applied].
Anusvāra and visarga arise from [the substitution of] *pūrṇaseva*.
When followed by another vowel, the *na* in the words *vanaspati*, *kratu*, *śatru*, and *paridhi* becomes *ra*, and *anusvāra* likewise.

The *anusvāra* [is substituted] for the letter *m* when followed by *repha* (r) or an *ūṣman* (sibilants and *h*). It occurs at the end of a word (*apādanta*), as in *agaḥ*, *aras*, and *anityavat*; it also occurs at the end of a *gaṇa* (group), as in *tvādgasavitus* and *tvādgahi*, and *tvadgahi*—these are the illustrations.

In the middle of a word, the *nakāra* and likewise the *makāra* become a *catva-anusvāra* before sibilants (*ūṣman*) that are not followed by the letter *repha*. Therefore, the preceding *anusvāra* is also an illustration of the correct pronunciation.

If the *pūrvapada* ends in *adguṇa* (a vowel other than *a*), then that very [vowel] becomes *satva* (the substitution of *o*) in the middle of the word before suffixes beginning with *k* or *t*, provided they have an *uṣman* following; however, this does not occur when the suffix begins with *na* or *vi*. Nor does it occur before the suffix *maṇi*.
The *mahit* [is] the lord of those who are intoxicated with honey, the greatest slayer of Vṛtra;
he has emerged from the unchanging, never indeed undergoing transformation; in the middle of the word, there is always the *anusvāra* for the letter *m*, and likewise the letter *r*.
O wise one, you are the knower and the messenger;
the letter *m* is naturally elided before the words *rāṭ* and *rājya* when they follow. (12) Thus, *saṃmrāṭ* and *sāmrājye* are examples, as is the word *nābhi*. (13)

Thus ends the section on the addition of the *anusvāra*. Now begins the section on the absence of modification of the letter *n*. Furthermore, the vowel *a* does not occur after a word-final *n*, but rather [the nasal] *ṃ* arises.
There may be the elision of the letter *ka*, and the people would become without protection (*udghāram*);
even Mahendra and the men [would be affected], as there is another illustrative example:
"the horse and the hornless goat," by which the letter *ka* does not undergo modification.
When followed by a vowel, one obtains both *lab* and *ālab*;
likewise, one obtains *śiśumāra*. This is how it should be understood by those learned in the Vedas:
there is no modification of the letter *kā*, nor is there a transition into *vaisphanit*.
The occurrence of *vaispharya* (aspiration) before a vowel is not certain;
many words well-known in the *Prātiśākhya* are not written by me here now, for fear of making the book too voluminous.
From Agniṣṭha, from those [beings], from the mind, from nourishment,
from you indeed, and from the gods; from the three worlds and from you, there is the vision of Mitra and of men— these are the worlds of food for him who does not [despise].
When the word *udi* follows, there is the illustration of *mitrānudi*.
For the word *bhakṣān*, [the change occurs] in *yonasya* when followed by *tvā* and *āpnotau*; for *śrapayāni tau*, [it occurs] in *gṛhānupagṛhānaimi varcasvāham eva ca*. 6–7.

"Manuṣyān," "antarikṣam," "nabhasvān," "ārdradānu," "svargān," "pāman," "anaḍvān," and likewise "āśuḥ śatru-tanuyaṃ"—knowing these eight [names], one is indeed naked (nagna). 8. And [the name] "nagna" itself.
Such is his portion of the domestic animals and likewise of the wild ones;
thus may he not harm us with misfortunes, nor our rivals, nor Indra,
nor the Virūpas, nor the Yātudhānas— may the God protect us from them.

Likewise, there is no modification of the *na* in *naḍvān*, *adhorāmaḥ*, and *vikāraḥ*, provided that these words stand before [the following word] and a vowel follows them. Thus ends the section on the absence of modification of the letter *na*.
Now follows the junction of *hal* consonants:

at the end of a word, *bh* becomes *y*; before *b*, *l*, and nasalized sounds (*anunāsika*), it remains; and before *y*, *v*, and *l*, as well as in the words *sarppaiḥ*, *miṣam*, *vāntam*, and the verse itself, [the rules apply].
When a consonant follows the letter *m*, the fifth letter of the following consonant's class is substituted;
as in "yāmiṣuṅ giriśantaiva" and "vrataṃ kṛṇuta eva ca.
Likewise, one shall perform the vow according to the rule: "from joint to joint," and so forth.

This [word] *pitṛbhyaḥ* becomes *pitṛbhyas* before *te*, and *vitta* becomes *vitte* before *am*. The letter *t* certainly undergoes the substitution of *l* when followed by the letter *gha*, as in *darśanam*; and the letter *t* at the end of a word likewise undergoes the substitution of *l* when the letter *l* follows.
The attainment [of the vowel], the imitation [of the consonant], and the nasalized *la*—
these three worlds, as well as "in this world," are the illustrations;
and the *ka*-sounds are separated from the *ṅa*-sounds by the two *ta*-sounds.
In the beginning of a word, there may be three *samudra* [consonants],
or even more than that; and when a vowel follows the letter *k*, even if it is separated by *n*, such is the *saṃhitā* among words— thus we declare according to the Vedic meters.
When the letter *cha* follows the words *sahayasya*, *atihāya*, and *ibhya*, there is always an elision (*pinasyu*) of the *e* [of *eti*] even when there is an intervening *ca*.
That which is the shadow (*chāyā*) and that which is dead (*mṛta*), as well as the word *chaṃdas*, [follow the same rule]. 7–8.

Shining forth, you are free from envy; may they strengthen you against all enemies. You are the conqueror of all quarters and the one who stands above; you are the sovereign of all plants—both those dwelling here and those beyond.
And *cāpyūṣmāṃ* in the words that have been mentioned;
*paraḥ*, *saṃbhavam*, *manthī*, *pṛthivīm*, and *śukraḥ* likewise; and after *pṛthivyāḥ*, there should be *svarāntam* in the words that have been mentioned. 10–11.

And in *viśvā vo brahma*, *viśvāharī*, *viśvājajāna*, *ca te śaphānām*, *tu kam*, *ceti*, and in these as well as in the following [verses], the word *imāḥ* ending in a vowel is certainly [to be treated] with these two [preceding words].
12. *havotābhyām*. *Imāḥ* ending in a vowel shall certainly [be joined] with these two.
Even when there is a boil, let it not be difficult for the physician;
may the grace of the gods release us from this as well. And may the Nāsatyas, dwelling in the highest realms, surely protect us from those [dangers] that end in death.
"O Tāviṣphoṭas, protect us; O Tātā, O physicians, likewise; O Tānas, O Tāvitānas, be gracious to us; O Tāthādevas, O Tānāsatyas, O Tāvabhūs, [protect us]. (15)

The word *sādhyāśīḥ* ending in *svar* (su) occurs in the context of the oblation (*havis*) for the couple; when the *sādhyāśīḥ* has received the oblation, the husband and wife partake of it. The word *dhiṣṭyā*, ending in *svar*, occurs in the phrase "you two [grant] wide space" (*varivo yuvam*).
In the word *dhiṣṇyā*, when followed by the letter *ya* or when the letter *ra* follows, the final visarga is elided; furthermore, the preceding short vowel invariably becomes long. 18.
*Rurū*, *raudra*, *rayīḥ*, *rāyaḥ*, *nīra-pāṅsi*, and *mṛkṣyataṃ*.
(18) The letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, the letter *ha*, and the last three consonants of each varga are designated as *ṣṭi*; these, together with the letter *ra*, total exactly twenty. (19)
And when followed by the letter *ra*, the visarga assumes both forms;
for example, in the words *agnirepha* and *akṣareṇāgneḥ*, there is the illustration: "Thou art the body of Agni.
There is also the illustration in *agnirmā* and *vinirvāmamantaregne*.
When a *visarga* preceded by a guttural (*kaṣṭhya*) encounters a vowel (*svara*), it undergoes *yama*;

however, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *ya*, and the *ya*-sound becomes resonant with the *ṛ*-tone (*riphita*). For example: *yā oṣadhīḥ* (where *yāḥ* becomes *yā*), and *indra ekaṃ tānāvocaṃ* (where *tān* becomes *tān*).
21. *yā oṣadhīriṃdra ekaṃ tāna āvokamityapi*.
The visarga preceded by *kavarga* (velar consonants) is elided when followed by *dyau*.
However, the elision of a *riphita* visarga does not occur when *dyau* follows. (Examples:
*devā yajñam ayakṣmāmakārṣṭa* and *punaḥ manaḥ*.
The retroflex *ṭa*-group and the dental *ta*-group at the end of a word, when followed by a consonant of their own respective groups,
definitely attain the status of the palatal *ca*-group according to their respective order;
that eye, being near, perceives the entire world as consciousness alone.
Whatever is the *āchachandaḥ* and whatever is the illustration from the waking state (25),
when the *tavarga* at the end of a word stands before the letter *śa*, it undergoes that same *tavarga*; thus, the substitution of *cha* for *śa* is prescribed (26).
The letter *śa* that follows a consonant (*sparśa*) does not invariably undergo the change to *cha*, just as in the examples:
*svadhāvāñchukraḥ*, *taccakṣuruchviṣaḥ*, *ucchrayā dadhācchradhyām*, and *tacchakeyaṃ nidarśanam*. (27)

The *s* of the root *stabhnāti* following *udaḥ* undergoes elision. When a consonant other than the fifth letter of a class follows, provided it is preceded by a vowel, that [consonant] becomes the third letter of its respective class. Bring this [word] upward from the subsequent [section].

Whatever [consonant] occurs in a *grāma*, and likewise in a *vamśa* or *muśadūmi*, for a non-fifth *sparśa*, its own fifth of the same class shall be substituted; and before a following fifth *sparśa*, it becomes *vāṅmāttyabaṇmahīm̐s*. 29–30.
The illustration is: "tan-mitrasya ca yan-me ca tan-me ca" (30).
From the third consonant (*sparśa*) that has been reached, and even from the fifth, there shall be the fourth [consonant] of the preceding *hakāra* (31).
"Uddharṣaya," "tathā caiva," "avāḍhavyāni," and "vāgghutaḥ"—
thus ends the section on vowel sandhi (svarasaṃdhi) concerning the combination of consonants (hal-saṃdhi).

When the letter *u* follows, every *visarga* that has *a* as its preceding vowel likewise undergoes the change to *o* when another vowel follows; however, this change occurs invariably only when a vowel follows, and it does not occur for a *riphita* (aspirated) *visarga*. Examples are:
*devo vaḥ agre* [becomes] *devo vo 'gre*, and *guvo agre* [becomes] *gavo 'gre*; *devaḥ agniḥ* [becomes] *devo 'gniḥ*. This is the illustration.

The word *eṣa*, when followed by the letter *ha* with a *visarga* as its penultimate (*upadhā*), invariably undergoes the change to *o*; likewise, it becomes *o* before *hadeva*. Furthermore, the *visarga* of the word *svar* also undergoes the change to *u* before *ruhau*.
The elision of the word *gavyūti* occurs even when the word *rātri* follows; likewise, for words beginning with *ahar*, there is the elision of *ahorātra* and *ahorātrāḥ*.
In the case of the *y*-class and *v*-class [consonants], *y* and *v* respectively shall take their place when followed by a non-homogeneous vowel.
*Tryambakaḥ* and *vīḍvaṅgaḥ* are examples; likewise, *indra* [is an example].
When the four vowels *e*, *o*, *ai*, and *au* are followed by the consonants *t*, *y*, *v*, *y*, *v*, and *y* respectively, they undergo these changes when a vowel stands immediately after. (4–5)

In the case of *ilā* and *ihi*, when followed by *ga*, *iṣṭau*, *ca*, *etāvān*, or *ucitau*, there shall be elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel of those two words before a following vowel. Furthermore,
the *va* of *asau* is not elided before a consonant.
That [vowel] of yours, indeed, shall undergo elision when followed by *c*, *t*, *v*, or *r*. A guttural vowel certainly becomes short before the vowel *ṛ*;
for example: *viśvakarmarṣiḥ svāhā* and *ṛṣabham*. 8.

When followed by a vowel, the letter *a*, the letter *i*, and the letter *u* invariably undergo a long substitution in place of both [the preceding and following sounds] when followed by a consonant. (9) Examples are:
*tvāśābhyaḥ*, *ca*, *vihīṃ*, *iddhro*, *nūjjepantu*, and *nidarśanam*. (10)
When a guttural consonant meets the vowel *i*, and both reside in the same place of articulation, the letter *e* arises there; this is seen in the case of *varuṇe heti*.
Furthermore, when a guttural follows the vowel *u*, the letter *o* arises even for those who are fierce (*ugriyoḥ*).
"iha ṛjyamo tavīrāṃśca svāhā" is the illustration for *ū*.
When an *e* vowel follows an *a* vowel, and likewise when an *o* vowel follows an *a* vowel, they respectively become *ai* and *au*; as in "praitu brahmaṇaḥ. (12–13)

And likewise, they approached Indra’s waters, as well as the plants; and with the *Indraujasvat* mantra, they sprinkled the Puruṣa as a representative example. Indeed, they did not sprinkle him with the waters of the ocean.
That mantra is both short and long; in the case of both [the preceding and following vowels], the form of the subsequent one occurs, and therein it is the sublater of the preceding one alone.
Indeed, when a vowel ending in *a* (avarṇa) is followed by a vowel beginning with *jha*, the *ja* and *ha* are dropped even when followed by a red (*rakta*) vowel.

For both [vowels], the single substitute form (pararūpa) occurs invariably according to the first school of thought. However, when *ūti* follows a vowel other than *u*, the substitution of *o* occurs for both positions as well;
this is established as an invariable rule, as illustrated by the example "ṣaṣṭhauhī."
In uncombined vowels and before the letter *ṛ*, the substitution of *ā* for both [vowels] is certain;
likewise, in the case of *ārtti* and *jarā*, there is the example of *ārśyā* and *nṛśyā*. Furthermore, in the *Yajus* formulas, when preceded by *e* or *o*, the preceding form [of the vowel] occurs.
The nature of the Ṛkṣu and Bhāva is heard far from us;
may those three who are free from desire toward us behold him.
Who is the one who establishes the firm seat? The two Hotṛ-priests, the Earth, and Svadhā.
These [worlds], beginning with the *jyā*, are certainly manifest by their very nature:
the downward, the upward, and likewise the intermediate directions;
and this earth exists below, as well as in these other [directions]. 20–21.
A dual ending in *u*, likewise one in *ī*, and a dual ending in *e* shall certainly be *pragṛhya*. Furthermore,
when the vowel *o* occurs at the end of a word (*padānta*), it is also [a *pragṛhya*].
Then, having grasped *saṃjñā*, one should utter it without omission;
a word consisting of a single phoneme shall certainly be known as *apṛkta*. Furthermore, *ukāra* is known as *apṛkta*, as are *tve*, *asme*, *ca*, *amū*, and *camū*.
Let there be for these the designation *pragṛhya*, as well as for my *udātta* [vowel]. And that word which is *pragṛhya* shall remain in its original form (*prakṛti*) before a following vowel:
*indrāgnī āgatam svārthe* and *anyānyāmo ahaṃtava*. (24–25)
These two words *rodasī* and *ime* are always produced in their original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by a sound [other than a vowel].
Furthermore, the vowel *a*, when not joined with another consonant (*asparśa*), is also produced in its original form.
These two, as well as a protracted (*pluta*) vowel, are always produced in their original form when followed by another [sound].

The letter *o* at the end of a word remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by the vowel *i*. In the case of the words *viśya*, *ṛtta*, and *iva*, it always remains in its original form when followed by the word *śabda* in the sense of "encircling" (*veṣṭane*). Thus ends the section on Vowel Sandhi (*svarasaṃdhiprakaraṇa*).
Now begins the section on *avagraha*: A consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) following a vowel is reduplicated starting from its first letter;
however, a consonant following either the letter *ra* or the letter *ha* is reduplicated [from the beginning of the cluster]. (1)
"taj juṣasva yaviṣṭhya," likewise "śoca yaviṣṭhya," and "bhur bhuvaḥ suvar" joined with "martyeṣṭhāya"— these are the established [mantras],
including the word "iti" when it occurs at the beginning of a phrase, but the word alone when it stands independently.
The two Saṃhitās, consisting of various mantras, are said to be "sthitopasthita" (fixed and joined).
Whatever word occurs as a result of phonetic change, no modification arises for the preceding element when followed by the suffix "iti. 3–4.
Furthermore, in the *carcā* (repetition), two [words] are recited as indeclinables (*avyaya*):
"dve" and "dve," as well as "śīrṣe," "ūrū," and "bāhū"; and "amī," "tve," "tve," "camū," and "asme"—these are the illustrations. 5.

Furthermore, in the *saṃhitā*, these words— *svaraṃtaḥ* and *savitaḥ*— are seen without being separated [by an avagraha], even when devoid of the letter *r*. In that context, there shall be no avagraha for dual forms ending in the dual case-suffix.
If the preceding word does not end in a consonant, only then does that [sandhi] apply:
*indrāgnī*, *indrāvāyū*, and likewise *indrābṛhaspatī*;
as well as *indrāgnī*, *indravāyū*, *dudhukṣan*, and *sīṣadhāni*.
Dustara produced Prāvapya and likewise Sāsaka;
Bṛhaspati produced the Traiṣṭubha meter, and he fashioned day and night.
Āsīdaṣada and Bhaiṣāda were born, and they rejoice in the sacrificial grass (*śamī*).
Thus ends the book.
